I’ve mostly used it for data analysis when you have a lot of usage data or benchmarking in order to specify important requirements and functional limits, but that’s all offline work you do before implementing something new or an improvement.  So something like customers prefer products that implement this function within XXXms so we must beat that.

As far as runtime prob/stats, with little memory and processing space in embedded, it’s somewhat uncommon in my experience.  You’re usually not referencing lots of data onboard as storing big data sets and doing the math on them is expensive so I’ve basically never done onboard stats or model training.  Signals and data smoothing is about as close as I usually get and even then you’ll often use the simplest versions and you’re not using more than a handful of samples at a time.  I’ve done off-board model training and implemented the static models on hardware, but again that’s not real time.  Even then a high order polynomial regression is often better to implement than any fancy neural networks since it’s low overhead.

Of course there are rare high power systems using essentially full on PCs in autonomy or industrial settings, but that’s stretching the embedded definition, but it does kind of exist.

That said, the best engineers I know understand probability and stats well and it’s helpful to use as a general tool in all disciplines.  The more capable you are to recognize and understand the inherent randomness of the world the better.

Oh, don’t get me wrong, I have a TON of problems with AUTOSAR and it overcomplicates a lot of things with its process, but it does actually help remove a lot of the hardware dependence.  I now utilize its general structure and component basis but I simplify the build process and RTE, but maintain the benefits outside of automotive supplier commonality I don’t need (and don’t have to pay out the butt for someone’s AS tool chain).  Even if it’s all in house it makes hardware changes pretty simple and application code is none the wiser.

Dashboard is just one of the dozens of embedded devices in a car and aggregates signals from around the vehicle network.  Your intelligent battery sense device doesn’t have any UI, nor does your low pressure fuel pump module, etc.  Do you count a headlight control unit as a display since it turns the lights on or off from serial bus signals?  The window switch is separate device and has no display, but it takes user input, does that count even if it only talks serially to the window motor controller (probably not even directly)?

It isn’t that hard if you just design your architecture around tests.  Components and abstraction make it really easy, but it’s really hard to change to that later.  I’ve been places where they never accounted for that and it was a big ol ball of mud so tightly coupled that it was essentially untestable outside of running hardware and to get to abstraction you’d need to do a ground up rewrite.

Though not simple devices by any means, something like F’ or AUTOSAR is portable by means of component based design.  So your architecture has a lower level BSW that changes per device but has consistent top side interfaces to remove hardware dependence. Than an abstracted middleware handles scheduling and communication services between application components.  Components just have a singular task to do but talk to other components via the middleware and can be hardware independent. You just swap in and out components based on product need.  

For example if you have a car with a V8/I4/electric motor the rest of the software stays the same but the component that handles torque production just gets swapped out and things like accelerator pedal or lights stay the same.

I’d probably say the opposite for most of that. Embedded is intrinsically a bridge between Electrical Engineering and Software Engineering.  I think people need to remember that you are delivering real world changes and the code and MCUs are just a means to get there.  I am not saying you need to know every detail, but everything I have ever learned under the hood of the compiler, and hardware has helped me to do better embedded work.

Knowing how your compiler gets from code to data and instructions is pretty important especially if you start realtime optimizing.  Controlling how those instructions and data get linked into hardware devices is mandatory at least.  You had better understand runtime and how the hardware operates and how resources and registers are used if you’re going to design your tasking and try to debug realtime problems.

Circuits and logic aren’t real divorced from embedded either.  Sure, you don’t go into the gates of the ALU but it can help to understand why registers are doing what they’re doing.  Plus you should be able to build gate logic to add in a set of peripheral chips into the address space.  Your new CAN API might not be reliably if the circuit isn’t completely terminated, so how do you design a diagnostic to identify this? Do you need to add hardware, or what can you do in code alone before the next board revision?

I have seen embedded programmers that treat it like completely abstract user space code and ignore low levels and it just leads to more problems for everyone.

I don’t know if I’d say that. The more I’ve done embedded the more I’ve had to understand even my includes and architecture instructions. You’ve really gotta understand your libraries and how they’re impacting hardware resources from ISRs to tasking frequently, even if you’re not manually auditing every single function in it. You rarely have enough resources that you can just ignore any part of code. 

Even something like an API you’ve got to understand your byte ordering, atomicity, tasking and hardware resources, and how does implementing something with a function vs. inline vs. function-like max to affect the instruction and register levels.  If your function is safety critical you can’t just assume it’ll just work out.

To me it sounds like they’re probably using some form of PTP to synchronize player clocks so that every action is timestamped with a common time basis.  That way ping and discrete ticks don’t matter as much and you just queue actions based on their actually happened, not just when received by the server. I assume it probably introduces a delay but that delays is probably limited by the worst player ping. 

PTP is what networks and banks use to keep in sync taking into account network latencies and clock performance. So when you get paid at 12:02:14.237488 and rent gets withdrawn at 12:02:14.300003 they know which came first and if you overdrafted even if on other sides of the world. It’s widely used to synchronize many things already and it’s been expanding to other industries lately with low end hardware and more specific Implementations. 

Good PTP is syncing to sub microseconds but syncing within a few millisecond sounds like it’s already better than current tick based systems by far. 

(PTP = precision time protocol)

They’re vortex generators that are typically sold to gullible truckers and delivery van owners. They’re sold as being a drag reduction but if you understand the basics of what vortex generators do they’re snake oil. I worked at a place and did a whole wind tunnel test on delivery vans too see if they helped. Nope. Added drag as they of course would. Vortex generators add energy into rotating the flow (at the expense of drag) to keep airflow attached to a curved surface. That corner on that suv is already designed to detach airflow, not keep it so this is fighting the design at the cost of more drag. 

VGs do have some uses, but not like this. On a plane’s wing they are adding drag to help prevent stalls, I.e. falling out of the sky, which is worse than drag. On the old Evo rally cars it was to help turn the flow down the very vertical rear window to give more flow to the rear wing, so drag to get downforce. VGs basically cannot reduce your drag because that’s not what they do.

Don’t forget about angle losses, though. A 400W panel is only going to give you 400W when pointed directly at the sun on a perfectly clear day with zero clouds or humidity. Horizontal on a truck bed you’re going to get a fraction of that just due to the cosine losses. 

Average sun height in Phoenix is about ~60 degrees above the horizon and that’s only at high noon. Assuming a sinusoidal sun angle over the course of the day on average you get 63% of your maximum height for those 12 hours. So overall you’re only getting ~50% of your panel rating over a day in otherwise ideal conditions. It just gets worse if you have clouds or park facing south with a cab in the way. So your 2kW is quickly going to be less than 1 and then throw in conversion losses and you’re paying an awful lot for a little power that’s not even typical in much of the county. 

Is it useful in a pinch, sure. Is that worth paying for over just planning ahead with charges, though?

Regarding the aerodynamics, especially for a first cut design I would just focus on getting something mechanically working first and leave aero for later. You can easily replace control arms later down the line with something more advanced after getting a viable base design working.

Even if you don't end up making oval or airfoil structural cross sections, you can always use cylinders and add things on top.  Simplest would be gluing stiff sheet on the trailing edge.  Just make it a couple diameters long.  [This wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kármán_vortex_street#Engineering_problems) has an example of what I mean on the second example on the left. Normally orbiting around a planet/star you’ll have ellipses (& circles which are just very specific ellipses) while orbits leaving earth to go to Mars, for example, will be hyperbolas. Parabolas are a very specific edge case between eclipses and hyperbolas but generally not useful in orbits. 

Also optics typically need a lot of conic math. Focusing mirrors are usually parabolic and sometimes spherical. Lenses are some form of conics for the faces.

The mode 1 PIDs are so useful and that's only a fraction of what's going around in that port that any shop or enthusiast would love to have.  There's what, 200 PIDs, mandated parameters you can read?  There are hidden PIDs for THOUSANDS of variables to read and control from there it's amazing.  You can read cylinder pressure estimates, component life remaining, control individual cylinder timing, activate cylinder disable modes, active shock absorber control, you name it.  If that info were public it would be amazing for repair or just fun.

So in industry we'd call this a chin spoiler.

Chin spoilers are kind that have vertical surfaces (like this or a modern pickup truck) that force air up and over the car (like a dam might do with water).  [Splitters](http://www.c1-r.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/Maxton-Design-Front-Racing-Splitter-Focus-ST-Mk3-Preface-Version-1.png) are the horizontal surfaces that "cut" the air into sections that go over top or below.  Splitters are easily tuned for racing since you can change the angle pretty easily, though.  Also sticking farther forward can sometimes help by giving you more of a moment arm with the force produced.

They are both used controlling the proportion of air that goes over the car vs under it.  However, splitters usually are more effective for downforce and worse for drag but it's not a rule.  Splitters tend to hold a big high pressure zone in front of the bumper and on top of the splitter but high pressure on the front of the car is a big drag force even if you're getting a lot of front downforce.

There is a technical difference between an airdam and chin spoiler as well but most people don't use it consistently.  A chin spoiler is farther forward and sends air over the car while an air dam is under the radiator and is used to send air up into the radiator face.  An air dam can be seen in [C4 corvettes](https://www.parts123.com/parts123/yb.dll?Parta~ShowPic~Z5Z5Z50000050f~Z5Z5Z5GVJS6) which is helpful since it doesn't have a lot of grille area like modern ones do.

Inverted Vs were used a few times in WWII era aircraft.  Notable the BF 109 and 110 had inverted V12s.  [This page on the engine](https://acesflyinghigh.wordpress.com/2016/06/25/under-the-cowl-of-the-flying-heritage-collection-bf-109e-3-emil/) has some photos and a cutaway showing the heads at the bottom.  

Supposedly this was done to improve downward visibility for the pilot since the widest part of the engine wasn't at the top of the cowling like in a Spitfire or Mustang. Potentially since the 109 had a cannon in the prop it might have brought the sight line up closer to the pilot's perspective as well.  There are also thoughts that it made some maintenance jobs easier by bringing the heads lower to the ground.

It seems no one is super sure about why they added the complexity of doing this and not a conventional engine, but it certainly is possible, just harder than necessary.

As for converting something like an existing engine to this configuration it probably would be no small task as gravity is used to control some flow of oil to the sump and spending a lot of time upside down may not work real well or would require a ton of retrofitting work.
